column5: break fallow ground; sow righteousness; rain
column6: The commentary’s plough opening a hard surface for seed and water meets Hosea’s command to break fallow ground, sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, and await divine rain; it gives the field image an explicit ethical and God-dependent form.

column5: break fallow ground; do not sow thorns
column6: The commentary’s resistant surface that must be opened is matched by Jeremiah’s summons to break up fallow ground and not sow among thorns; it makes the agricultural opening a moral beginning.

column5: wash yourselves; remove evil
column6: The commentary reads tezekkâ as cleansing undertaken by the person; Isaiah commands hearers to wash themselves, make themselves clean, and remove evil deeds, giving that reflexive sense an ethical counterpart.

column5: circumcise yourselves; heart-foreskin
column6: Against self-certification, the commentary distinguishes undertaken cleansing; Jeremiah tells its hearers to circumcise themselves to YHWH and remove their heart-foreskin, supplying a heart-level image of such work.

column5: claim of a clean heart
column6: The commentary rejects self-proclaimed purity in tuzakkū anfusakum; Proverbs asks who can say that they have made their heart clean and are pure from sin, directly restraining that claim.

column5: turn from sins; do justice; live
column6: The commentary makes a person’s purification decisive for their end; Ezekiel’s wicked person turns from sin, keeps justice, and lives rather than dies, giving an individual ethical life-and-death judgment.

column5: individual righteousness and guilt
column6: The commentary’s men excludes lineage as a guarantee and assigns the result to the acting person; Ezekiel denies transferred guilt and says righteousness or wickedness rests on its own bearer.

column5: God sprinkles clean water
column6: The commentary also says that purification rests on divine favor, not autonomous self-approval; Ezekiel has God sprinkle clean water and cleanse the people, supplying its complementary divine agency.

column5: cleanse ourselves; holiness in fear
column6: The commentary joins self-purification to inner fear; Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves from fleshly and spiritual defilement while completing holiness in fear of God, an unusually close ethical sequence.

column5: purifies himself in hope
column6: The commentary’s reflexive tezekkâ is closely echoed by the person who purifies himself because of hope; the verse makes awaiting the final good a present practice of cleansing.

column5: purified souls by obedience to truth
column6: The commentary treats purification as the response of one who receives admonition; 1 Peter describes souls purified through obedience to truth, adding received teaching and brotherly love to that process.

column5: no distinction; hearts purified by faith
column6: The commentary refuses ethnic membership as sufficient and also acknowledges divine purification; in the Gentile debate Acts says God made no distinction and purified hearts by faith, joining both features.

column5: work out salvation with fear and trembling
column6: The commentary presents felâh as personally labored for with inward fear; Philippians calls believers to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, a close effort-and-result formulation.

column5: God works willing and doing
column6: The commentary sets human self-work on ground prepared by God; the following claim that God works both willing and doing articulates the divine agency held alongside that work.

column5: salvation by mercy; washing of regeneration
column6: The commentary calls purification a person’s action while admitting grace; Titus grounds salvation in mercy and regenerative washing rather than works done in righteousness, a Christian counter-formulation whose different ground is material.

column5: cleansed hearts; washed body; draw near
column6: The commentary puts purification before remembrance and prayer; Hebrews has worshippers draw near with hearts cleansed from conscience and bodies washed, giving that order a worship-setting counterpart.

column5: self-abasement; declared justified
column6: The commentary says the purified person does not pronounce the final verdict on himself; Jesus declares the self-abasing tax collector justified rather than the self-exalting Pharisee, narrating that divine verdict.

column5: God repays each according to deeds
column6: The commentary calls kad eflaha a settled result of accounting; Paul’s statement that God repays each person according to deeds provides an explicit final-account counterpart.

column5: fruit worthy of repentance
column6: The commentary hears growth and moral cleansing together in tezekkâ; John’s demand for fruit worthy of repentance turns inner change into the crop-image of demonstrable action.

column5: do not rely on Abraham as father
column6: The commentary contrasts a named lineage or group with the action of whoever purifies himself; John forbids reliance on descent from Abraham, making the same exclusion concrete.

column5: whoever fears God and does righteousness is accepted
column6: The commentary’s men makes the criterion action rather than a people-name; Peter says that in every nation the one who fears God and does righteousness is accepted, a direct universal analogue.

column5: inward Jew; heart circumcision; praise from God
column6: The commentary opposes group-label and self-given judgment to real purification; Paul relocates Jewish identity to the heart and says its praise comes from God rather than people, sharpening both contrasts.

column5: God-fearing, almsgiving, continual prayer
column6: The commentary places fear, arınma in its giving sense, and prayer/remembering in one sequence; Cornelius is described through precisely God-fear, many alms, and continual prayer.

column5: prayers and alms as memorial before God
column6: The commentary brings cleansing, remembrance, and prayer together; Cornelius’s prayers and alms ascend as a memorial before God, making the divine reception of that pair explicit.

column5: give alms; all things clean
column6: The commentary develops zakāt as giving that cleanses and grows the giver; Jesus’ instruction to give alms so that all is clean gives a particularly direct almsgiving-and-cleansing parallel.

column5: righteousness performed to be seen; no reward
column6: The commentary contrasts showy giving on barren rock with giving for God; Jesus warns that righteousness performed to be seen by others has no reward from the Father, supplying the same moral distinction.

column5: almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin
column6: The commentary links giving, purification, and felâh from death into abiding good; Tobit says almsgiving both delivers from death and purges sin, making that threefold relation unusually explicit.

column5: almsgiving atones as water quenches fire
column6: The commentary’s rain and fertile soil image joins to cleansing through giving; Sirach compares almsgiving’s atonement to water extinguishing a blazing fire, extending both of those concrete images.

column5: the one who waters is watered
column6: The commentary calls giving an apparent decrease that becomes growth; Proverbs says the generous person is enriched and the one who waters is watered, giving the reversal an agricultural aphorism.

column5: pour yourself out for the hungry
column6: The commentary makes the crop’s due and charity part of purification; Isaiah makes care for the hungry the concrete act from which light rises, giving an ethical content to that fruitful giving.

column5: watered garden; unfailing spring
column6: The commentary’s receptive garden takes rain and bears growth; Isaiah promises the giver a life like a watered garden and a spring whose waters do not fail, turning provision into enduring fertility.

column5: forgotten harvest sheaf left for vulnerable people
column6: The commentary’s field includes the crop’s due being given away; Deuteronomy requires a forgotten sheaf be left for the resident alien, orphan, and widow, and links that harvest generosity to blessing on labor.

column5: seed to sower; multiplied seed; harvest of righteousness
column6: The commentary says that charity’s apparent loss is growth and that human cultivation does not cause growth by itself; Paul’s giver of seed multiplies sowing and increases a harvest of righteousness, combining both claims.

column5: one plants and waters; God gives growth
column6: The commentary distinguishes human ploughing from God’s making the crop grow; Paul’s plant-and-water image makes God, rather than the human workers, the giver of increase.

column5: blade, head, full grain
column6: The commentary insists that tezekkâ suggests step-by-step growth; Mark’s earth yields fruit in the stages blade, head, then full grain, giving that gradualness a kingdom parable.

column5: sowing to Spirit; reaping eternal life
column6: The commentary joins an act of self-purification to permanent good rather than the temporary world; Paul’s sowing image culminates in reaping eternal life, making the agricultural outcome explicitly enduring.

column5: give alms; unfailing heavenly treasure
column6: The commentary presents giving as a gain that lasts beyond the nearer life; Jesus couples alms with a treasure in heaven that does not fail, a direct giving-and-abiding-good correspondence.

column5: has eternal life; has passed from death to life
column6: The commentary reads kad eflaha as a final result announced as already settled; John likewise states a present possession and completed passage from death to life, while grounding it in hearing and believing rather than self-purification.

column5: everlasting life and everlasting contempt
column6: The commentary opposes a permanent good to the fire’s unliveable continuation; Daniel’s resurrection scene divides sleepers between everlasting life and enduring contempt, giving a Hebrew Bible two-destiny analogue.

column5: worm does not die; fire is not quenched
column6: The commentary’s preceding fate is an unending fire in which one neither dies nor lives; Isaiah’s final rebel scene supplies the enduring worm and unquenched fire that make such persistence horrific.

column5: worm does not die; fire not quenched
column6: The commentary’s fire contrast can be read with Jesus’ reuse of Isaiah’s undying-worm and unquenchable-fire formula; it shows the formula’s Christian punitive reception.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The commentary sets two continuing ends against each other, one good and one ruinous; Matthew closes its judgment scene with the same opposed pair of eternal punishment and eternal life.

column5: Aaron’s staff swallows the magicians’ staffs
column6: The commentary’s Moses scene has the object in his hand consume what the magicians produced; Exodus narrates Aaron’s staff swallowing their staffs, a direct shared contest detail.

column5: Pharaoh refuses to humble himself
column6: The commentary treats Pharaoh’s invitation to purify and fear as refused by a self-exalting ruler; Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH, giving the Hebrew narrative counterpart.

column5: greatness through being servant
column6: The commentary rejects the magicians’ definition of success as being above others; Jesus reverses rank in the same direction by defining greatness through service rather than rule over others.

column5: Moses rejects temporary enjoyment of sin
column6: The commentary’s Moses material contrasts the nearer life with what endures; Hebrews’ Christian reception says Moses chose affliction over sin’s temporary enjoyment, placing that contrast within Moses’ own story.

column5: Moses looks to reward over Egypt’s treasures
column6: The commentary says durable good, not present superiority, measures success; Hebrews reads Moses as valuing the coming reward above Egypt’s treasures, a Christian interpretive extension of that measure.

column5: rocky ground; no depth for root
column6: The commentary describes a sun-hardened surface where seed cannot take root; Mark’s rocky-ground seed has too little soil and no root, an indirect but concrete soil-reception parallel.

column5: good soil bears thirty-, sixty-, hundredfold
column6: The commentary contrasts a surface that sheds water with a garden that yields; Mark’s good soil produces an enlarged crop, providing the productive side of that contrast.

column5: tree by water; fruit; prospers
column6: The commentary layers furrowed growth under felâh without replacing its meaning of success; Psalm 1 makes the rightly instructed person a watered, fruit-bearing tree whose work prospers, a related success-through-fertility image.

column5: grass withers; God’s word stands forever
column6: The commentary sets green pasture that becomes refuse against the more abiding good and links it to received reminder; Isaiah contrasts fading grass with the word that stands forever, giving that temporal contrast a scriptural form.

column5: fruits in this world; principal in the world to come
column6: The commentary’s felâh means a good that remains beyond immediate life; this rabbinic valuation says certain deeds yield fruits now while their principal remains for the world to come, framing present action and enduring return together.

column5: repentance and good deeds; bliss of world to come
column6: The commentary opposes preference for the nearer life to a lasting final good; Avot distinguishes the irreplaceable time for repentance and good deeds now from the superior bliss of the world to come, refining that temporal contrast.

column5: Jannes and Jambres oppose Moses
column6: The commentary’s magicians contest Moses and calls their work a trick that cannot prosper; this later Christian naming tradition identifies Moses’ opponents as Jannes and Jambres and treats their opposition as resistance to truth.

column5: Hebrew zkr; God’s name as memorial
column6: For the commentary’s adjacent 87:15 dhikr, explicitly kept distinct from z-k-w, Hebrew zkr is a cognate memory-root: God calls his name his memorial to all generations in Moses’ call scene.

column5: Hebrew plh, pierce or split
column6: The commentary labels Arabic f-l-h’s concrete secondary sense as splitting earth; Hebrew plh, a cognate consonantal root, describes piercing or splitting in Job, confirming only that cleaving image rather than the ayah’s salvation sense.

column5: Hebrew zkh, cleanse hands
column6: The commentary’s z-k-w includes purification but warns against importing root senses; Job’s Hebrew zkh for cleansing hands is a possible cognate and a fragile lexical comparison, useful only as a cautious external instance of cleansing language.

column5: new heart and spirit; stone heart removed
column6: The commentary’s plough must open a resistant surface and its purification also depends on God; Ezekiel’s new heart and replacement of stone by flesh supplies a divine heart-softening counterpart to both details.

column5: YHWH circumcises the heart so that one may live
column6: The commentary holds together personal purification and a divine ground for it; Deuteronomy has God circumcise the heart for whole-hearted love and life, a Mosaic formulation of the latter side.

column5: washed, sanctified, justified in Lord’s name and Spirit
column6: The commentary says purification can be an act of God as well as of the person; Paul’s compact sequence of washing, sanctification, and justification gives that divine declaration a Christian form.

column5: cleansing by water with the word
column6: The commentary links warning, purification, and the messenger who recites and cleanses; Ephesians makes the word the means of Christ’s washing and sanctifying of the community.

column5: already clean because of the spoken word
column6: The commentary makes the received reminder part of the route to purification; Jesus tells the disciples that his spoken word has made them clean, a concise word-and-cleansing counterpart.

column5: put away filth; receive implanted word able to save
column6: The commentary moves from admonition received to self-purification and felâh; James joins putting away moral filth to receiving a word able to save the soul, preserving that full sequence.

column5: draw near; cleanse hands; purify hearts
column6: The commentary places purification before naming and praying to the Lord; James pairs drawing near to God with cleansing hands and purifying hearts, making the approach-and-cleansing relation explicit.

column5: all appear before judgment and receive for deeds
column6: The commentary calls kad eflaha a completed judgment result tied to what a person does; Paul’s judgment-seat statement gives each person a corresponding deed-based accounting.

column5: God brings every deed, good or evil, into judgment
column6: The commentary treats success as a verdict after a settled account rather than a group privilege; Ecclesiastes makes every hidden and visible deed subject to God’s judgment, supplying that universal reckoning.

column5: riches fail on the day of wrath; righteousness delivers from death
column6: The commentary contrasts near-world gain with purification that reaches safety from the final danger; Proverbs makes the same contrast between useless wealth at judgment and righteousness that delivers from death.

column5: seen things temporary; unseen things eternal
column6: The commentary opposes preference for the nearer life to the more abiding good; Paul’s visible-temporary and unseen-eternal distinction gives that contrast an explicit Christian formulation.

column5: full tithe and overflowing blessing
column6: The commentary’s zakāt sense is a required share whose apparent loss becomes growth; Malachi joins bringing the full tithe to the promise of an opened heaven and overwhelming blessing.

column5: Pharaoh refuses YHWH’s voice and denies knowing him
column6: The commentary’s Pharaoh declines the call to purification and claims illicit height; Exodus gives his shared narrative refusal in the question that denies YHWH’s authority and rejects obedience.

column5: do not fear; see YHWH’s deliverance
column6: The commentary’s Moses is told not to fear before the contest and defines success apart from dominating others; Moses’ sea-side exhortation makes deliverance a work to be seen from YHWH rather than a human victory claim.

column5: the seed grows though the sower does not know how
column6: The commentary distinguishes human tilling from growth beyond human command; Mark’s sower sleeps and rises while the seed sprouts without his knowing how, a necessary agency detail beside its staged crop image.

column5: no lasting city here; seek the coming city
column6: The commentary says the nearer life is not the abiding good; Hebrews’ contrast between no permanent city here and the one sought ahead gives that spatial, communal form to the same valuation.

column5: all flesh is grass and grass withers
column6: The commentary’s whole-surah setting sets pasture that becomes debris against what abides; Peter reapplies the fading-grass formula within Christian proclamation, a distinct reception of that image.

column5: God’s house of prayer for all peoples
column6: The commentary’s men refuses to reserve the saving path to one named community and proceeds to remembrance and prayer; Isaiah’s house of prayer for all peoples gives a temple-centered universal counterpart.

column5: R. Akiva: charity saves from Gehenna
column6: The commentary makes giving a purification linked to rescue from ruin; R. Akiva’s answer to Turnus Rufus treats charity as saving its giver through the poor from Gehenna, a rabbinic intensification of that claim.

column5: death, mourning, crying, and pain are no more
column6: The commentary contrasts the fire’s ongoing non-life with enduring good; Revelation’s final vision defines the positive end as a world where death and its accompaniments have ceased.
